danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Dette felttog bestod i en flugt af franskmændene, under hvilken de gjorde alt, hvad de kunne, for at ødelægge sig selv. Fra det øjeblik de drejede ind på Kalugavejen til den dag, deres anfører flygtede fra hæren, havde ingen af massens bevægelser nogen mening. Så man skulle tro, at historikerne, der tilskriver massens handlinger én enkelt mands vilje, ville have fundet det umuligt at få retræten til at passe ind i deres teori vedrørende denne periode af felttoget. Men nej! Bjerge af bøger er blevet skrevet af historikerne om dette felttog, og overalt beskrives Napoleons dispositioner, manøvrer og hans dybe planer, der styrede hæren, såvel som den militære genialitet, hans marskalker udviste.

Retræten fra Malo-Jaroslavets, da han havde en fri vej ind i et velforsynet distrikt, og parallelvejen lå åben for ham, langs hvilken Kutuzov (fyrst Kutuzov) siden forfulgte ham — denne unødvendige retræte ad en ødelagt vej — forklares for os som værende følgen af dybe overvejelser. Tilsvarende dybe overvejelser anføres for hans retræte fra Smolensk til Orsja. Derefter beskrives hans heltemod ved Krasnoje, hvor han angiveligt var rede til at tage imod et slag og personligt føre kommandoen, og skal have gået rundt med en birkepind og sagt:
»J'ai assez fait l'empereur; il est temps de faire le général,« * men alligevel straks løb igen og overlod de spredte rester af den hær, han efterlod, til deres skæbne.
* »Jeg har spillet kejser længe nok; nu er det tid til at spille general.«

Dernæst fortælles vi om marskalkernes sjælsstorhed, især Neys — en sjælsstorhed, der bestod i dette: at han om natten banede sig vej gennem skoven og over Dnepr og undslap til Orsja, idet han opgav faner, artilleri og ni tiendedele af sine mænd.

Og endelig fremstilles den store kejsers endelige afgang fra sin heroiske hær af historikerne som noget storslået og karakteristisk for geni. Selv den sidste flugt, der i dagligdags sprog betegnes som den dybeste usselhed, som ethvert barn lærer at skamme sig over — selv den handling finder retfærdiggørelse i historikernes sprog.

Når det er umuligt at strække de højst elastiske tråde i historisk spidsfindighed længere, når handlinger tydeligt strider mod alt, hvad menneskeheden kalder ret eller blot retfærdigt, fremfører historikerne et reddende begreb om »storhed«. »Storhed«, synes det, udelukker målestokke for ret og uret. For den »store« mand er intet forkert, der er ingen grusomhed, som en »stor« mand kan klandres for.

»C'est grand!« * siger historikerne, og så findes der ikke længere hverken godt eller ondt, men kun »grand« og »ikke grand«. Grand er godt, ikke grand er dårligt. Grand er kendetegnet, i deres opfattelse, for visse særlige dyr kaldet »helte«. Og Napoleon, der flygter hjem i en varm pelsfrakke og overlader dem, der ikke blot var hans kammerater men (efter hans mening) mænd, han havde ført dertil, til at gå til grunde, føler que c'est grand, *(2) og hans sjæl er rolig.
* »Det er storslået!«
*(2) At det er storslået.

»Du sublime (han så noget sublimt i sig selv) au ridicule il n'y a qu'un pas,« * sagde han. Og hele verden har i halvtreds år gentaget: »Sublimt! Storslået! Napoléon le Grand!« Du sublime au ridicule il n'y a qu'un pas.
* »Fra det ophøjede til det latterlige er der kun ét skridt.«
Og det falder ingen ind, at det at anerkende en storhed, der ikke kan måles med målestokken for ret og uret, blot er at indrømme sin egen tomhed og umådelige ringhed.
For os, med den målestok for godt og ondt Kristus har givet os, er ingen menneskelige handlinger umålelige. Og der er ingen storhed, hvor enkelhed, godhed og sandhed er fraværende.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: This campaign was essentially a flight during which the French did everything possible to destroy themselves. From the moment they turned onto the Kaluga road until the day their leader abandoned the army, not one movement of the mob made any sense. One might have expected that historians—who attribute the actions of the masses to the will of one man—would find it impossible to fit the story of this retreat into their framework. But no! Mountains of books have been written about this campaign, and everywhere we find descriptions of Napoleon's strategic arrangements, his maneuvers, and the deep plans that supposedly guided the army, as well as the military genius of his marshals.

The retreat from Malo-Yaroslavets, when Napoleon had a clear road into a well-supplied region and a parallel route that Kutuzov later followed—this needless retreat along a devastated road—is explained to us as the result of deep strategic thinking. Similarly profound reasoning is offered for his retreat from Smolensk to Orsha. Then his heroism at Krasnoe is described, where he supposedly stood ready to accept battle, took personal command, walked about with a birch stick, and said:
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general"—but then immediately ran away again, abandoning the scattered remnants of the army he left behind.
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general."

Then we are told of the greatness of soul of the marshals, especially of Ney—a greatness of soul that consisted in sneaking through the forest by night, crossing the Dnieper, and escaping to Orsha while abandoning his standards, artillery, and nine-tenths of his men.

And finally, the departure of the great Emperor from his heroic army is presented to us by historians as something noble and characteristic of genius. Even that final act of running away—which in plain language is the lowest depth of cowardice that every child is taught to be ashamed of—even that act finds justification in the historians' vocabulary.

When it becomes impossible to stretch the elastic threads of historical reasoning any further, when actions clearly violate everything humanity calls right or even just, historians produce their saving concept of "greatness." "Greatness," it seems, makes the standards of right and wrong irrelevant. For the "great" man, nothing is wrong; there is no crime for which a "great" man can be blamed.

"It is grand!" say the historians, and there is no longer any good or evil, only "grand" and "not grand." Grand is good, not grand is bad. Grand is the defining trait, in their view, of certain special creatures called "heroes." And Napoleon, escaping home in a warm fur coat while leaving his comrades—men he himself had brought there—to perish, feels that this is grand, and his conscience is at peace.
("It is grand.")
("That it is grand.")

"From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step," he said. And the whole world has been repeating for fifty years: "Sublime! Grand! Napoleon the Great!" From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.
("From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.")
And it occurs to no one that to accept a kind of greatness that exists outside the standards of right and wrong is simply to admit one's own insignificance and boundless moral smallness.
For us, with the standard of good and evil given us by Christ, no human actions are beyond judgment. And there is no greatness where simplicity, goodness, and truth are absent.
